V01.text: Every Halloween for seven years, at exactly eleven forty-seven at night, someone knocked on Walter Greene's door.

F001.text: It was always the same trick-or-treater. A small figure in a pumpkin mask, and a brown coat far too big for it.

F002.text: It never said trick or treat. It never said thank you. It just held out an old white pillowcase, and waited.

F003.text: And every year, Walter noticed the same impossible thing. The child never grew. Not an inch. Not in seven years.

F004.text: This is the story of an old man, a quiet little town in Vermont, and a trick-or-treater who came back every Halloween.

F005.text: And it's the story of what that old man found, when he finally decided to follow it home.

F006.text: This is the story of the last trick-or-treater of Maple Falls, Vermont. And it begins, of all things, with a scarecrow.

F007.text: Walter Greene lived in the same white farmhouse on Orchard Lane for twenty-six years. At the edge of town, where the houses ended and the fields began.

F008.text: He and his wife, Margaret, never had children of their own. So every Halloween, they made the whole town's children their own.

F009.text: Margaret baked caramel apples for three days straight. Walter carved pumpkins until his hands ached. The porch looked like a pumpkin patch.

F010.text: And every year, Walter wore the same costume. A scarecrow. Margaret had sewn it for him in 1962, their first Halloween in the house, straw hat and all.

F011.text: Kids from all over Maple Falls walked the long road to Orchard Lane, just to get a caramel apple from the scarecrow and his wife.

F012.text: In the spring of 1988, Margaret passed away in her sleep. She was sixty-six. The whole town came to say goodbye.

F013.text: That October, Walter didn't carve a single pumpkin. The porch stayed dark. The scarecrow costume stayed folded in the cedar chest upstairs.

F014.text: But on the morning of Halloween, a little girl from down the road left a drawing in his mailbox. A scarecrow, holding a caramel apple.

F015.text: Walter looked at that drawing for a long time. Then he went upstairs, opened the cedar chest, and took out the straw hat.

F016.text: He couldn't make caramel apples the way Margaret did. So he drove to the store and bought the biggest chocolate bars they had.

V02.text: That night, the scarecrow of Orchard Lane opened his door again. And the children came, just like always.

F017.text: It was a good night. The best he'd had since spring. Witches, cowboys, and a tiny astronaut who made him laugh until he had to sit down.

F018.text: By eleven, the last of the kids had gone home. Walter sat on the porch swing in his scarecrow costume, with half a bowl of candy left.

F019.text: He talked to Margaret for a while. Out loud. He told her about the astronaut. He told her he missed her. The field was silent.

F020.text: At eleven forty, he blew out the candles and went inside. He hung the straw hat on the hook by the door, and put the kettle on.

F021.text: At exactly eleven forty-seven, there was a knock. Three soft knocks. Low on the door, too low for a grown-up. Walter looked at the clock.

V03.text: On the porch stood a child in a papier-mache pumpkin mask, holding out an old white pillowcase.

F022.text: The mask was homemade. Faded orange paint, a crooked painted smile, two dark holes for eyes. The kind of mask nobody had made in decades.

F023.text: The child wore a man's brown wool coat, so big the sleeves were rolled up four times, and the hem dragged on the porch boards.

F024.text: Walter smiled and asked where the child's folks were. It was awfully late. The child didn't answer. It just held the pillowcase a little higher.

F025.text: So Walter dropped in a chocolate bar. For a second, a breath of cold air came out of the pillowcase. Like air from a cellar.

F026.text: The child turned and walked down the steps. Not toward the road, where the houses were. Toward the empty field behind the house.

F027.text: Walter grabbed his flashlight and called after it. But by the time he reached the steps, the field was empty. Just grass and moonlight.

F028.text: He told himself it was a neighbor's kid playing a prank. And he kept telling himself that for almost a year.

F029.text: Halloween, 1989. Walter wore his scarecrow costume again. The kids came again. And at exactly eleven forty-seven, there were three soft knocks.

F030.text: Same pumpkin mask. Same brown coat, with the sleeves rolled up four times. Same white pillowcase. Walter's heart started pounding.

F031.text: This time he noticed something else. The coat was damp. Not from rain, it hadn't rained in weeks. It smelled like cold, wet stone.

F032.text: He put a chocolate bar in the pillowcase and watched the child walk toward the field. This time, he followed it to the fence.

F033.text: It walked straight into the tall grass. The grass didn't move. The dry leaves didn't crunch. And halfway across the field, it was just gone.

V04.text: It walked into the field without bending a single blade of grass. And then, it simply wasn't there anymore.

F034.text: Walter didn't sleep that night. He sat at the kitchen table with a notebook, and wrote down everything he could remember.

F035.text: The time. The coat. The smell. The way the smile on the mask was painted a little crooked on the left. He dated the page. October 31st, 1989.

F036.text: Halloween, 1990. Walter waited by the door with his notebook. At eleven forty-seven, three soft knocks. He wrote down the time before he opened the door.

F037.text: The year before, he had marked the child's height on the porch post with a pencil. He checked it again. Exactly the same.

F038.text: Halloween, 1991. The same. Halloween, 1992. The same. The kids who came earlier in the evening were growing up. They got taller every year.

F039.text: But the child in the pumpkin mask stayed exactly the same height. Four feet and two inches. Year after year after year.

F040.text: In 1992, Walter finally asked. What's your name, son? The child raised one small hand in the wool sleeve, and pointed at the field.

V05.text: It didn't say a word. It only pointed at the field. And Walter understood that it wanted him to follow.

F041.text: But Walter was seventy-two, the field was dark, and something in him was afraid. So he closed the door. And he hated himself for it.

F042.text: That winter, he started asking questions. Carefully. He didn't want the town to think the old scarecrow had lost his mind.

F043.text: He asked his neighbors if a family with a little boy lived nearby. Nobody knew of one. Not on Orchard Lane. Not for a very long time.

F044.text: So he drove to the Maple Falls public library and asked the librarian to help him look through the old newspapers on microfilm.

F045.text: He didn't know what he was looking for. So he started with Halloween. Every November first, of every year, going back as far as they had.

F046.text: It took him three weeks. Then, in the paper from November 2nd, 1951, he found a headline that made his hands go cold.

F047.text: Local boy missing on Halloween night. Nine-year-old Billy Harlan. Last seen walking alone on Orchard Lane, at about a quarter to midnight.

F048.text: There was a photograph. A small, freckled boy grinning at the camera, holding up a homemade papier-mache pumpkin mask. The same mask.

F049.text: The article said Billy had worn his late father's brown wool coat that night, because it was cold. Sleeves rolled up four times.

F050.text: Walter sat in the dark library for a long time. The boy had been gone for forty-one years. And he was still out trick-or-treating.

F051.text: The article mentioned Billy's older sister, Dorothy. It took Walter two months, but he found her. A retired schoolteacher living in Burlington.

F052.text: He almost didn't go. What could he possibly say? Your little brother knocks on my door every Halloween? She'd call the police on him.

F053.text: But in March of 1994, he drove up to Burlington with a box of chocolates, and the old newspaper clipping folded in his coat pocket.

F054.text: Dorothy Harlan was small and sharp-eyed. She looked at the clipping, then at Walter, and said quietly: You've seen him. Haven't you?

F055.text: Walter told her everything. The knocks. The mask. The pillowcase. The field. She listened without interrupting, holding his hand the whole time.

F056.text: Then she told him what happened in 1951. Billy had begged to go out alone that year. Just once. He was nine. He was big enough, he said.

F057.text: He wanted to go to one last house. The old Kessler farmhouse, out past the end of Orchard Lane. The Kesslers always gave out popcorn balls.

F058.text: The Kessler house burned down in 1960, two years before Walter moved in. Today it was just an empty field. The field behind his house.

F059.text: Dorothy said the whole town had searched for a month. The woods, the river, every barn and cellar in Maple Falls. They never found anything.

F060.text: Their mother never moved away. Every Halloween until the day she died, she left the porch light on all night, in case Billy found his way home.

F061.text: Before he left, she squeezed his hand. Please, she said. If he comes again, go with him. He's been waiting a long time for someone to follow.

V06.text: Dorothy Harlan had waited forty-three years for an answer. She asked Walter for only one thing: to follow him.

F062.text: Halloween, 1994. Walter was seventy-four. He put on the scarecrow costume one more time, and handed out candy to the children, just like always.

F063.text: At eleven thirty, he put on his warm boots, put new batteries in his flashlight, and sat by the door with his coat on.

F064.text: The field behind the house was silver with frost. The moon was full. A thin fog was lying low over the grass, like water.

F065.text: At eleven forty-seven, three soft knocks. Walter opened the door. The small figure in the pumpkin mask was standing there, holding out its pillowcase.

F066.text: Walter dropped in a chocolate bar. Then he knelt down, so the mask was level with his eyes, and said quietly: Okay, Billy. Show me.

V07.text: For the first time in seven years, the child didn't vanish. It walked slowly into the fog. And Walter followed.

F067.text: They crossed the field together. The old man in the scarecrow hat, and the small figure in the pumpkin mask, side by side in the fog.

F068.text: The grass around Walter crunched with frost. Around the child, there was no sound at all. Walter's breath came out in white clouds. The child's didn't.

F069.text: Halfway across, the fog grew thicker. Walter could barely see his own hands. But the pumpkin mask seemed to glow faintly, just ahead of him.

F070.text: Then the child stopped. In the middle of the field was something Walter had walked past a hundred times, and never really seen.

F071.text: An old stone well. Covered with rotting gray boards. Half hidden by weeds and brambles. It must have belonged to the Kessler farm.

V08.text: The child pointed down at the boards. Then, right before Walter's eyes, it faded into the fog.

F072.text: Walter stood alone in the field. On the gray boards of the well lay the old white pillowcase. And beside it, the pumpkin mask.

F073.text: He picked up the mask with trembling hands. The papier-mache was soft and damp. The inside smelled like cold, wet stone. Just like the coat.

F074.text: He didn't try to open the well. He sat down on the frosty grass beside it, holding the mask in his lap, and waited for morning.

F075.text: At sunrise, he walked back to the house, still wearing the straw hat, and called the county sheriff.

F076.text: Sheriff Tom Brady had known Walter for thirty years. He didn't laugh. He looked at the mask for a long time, and then he made some calls.

F077.text: By noon, there were trucks in the field. Men with ropes and lights pulled the gray boards off the old Kessler well, for the first time in decades.

F078.text: The well had been dry for decades. At the bottom, under forty-three autumns of leaves, they found what the whole town had searched for in 1951.

F079.text: Billy had fallen into the old well in the dark that night, on his way to one last house. After forty-three years, he could finally come home.

F080.text: Billy Harlan was laid to rest in November of 1994, next to his mother and father, in the old Maple Falls cemetery on the hill.

F081.text: Dorothy drove down from Burlington. Walter walked beside her up the hill, through the red and yellow leaves.

F082.text: She asked Walter to put one thing in with her brother. Not flowers. The pumpkin mask. He'd want it, she said. It was his favorite.

F083.text: After the service, she held Walter's hand and cried. Thank you, she said. You're the only one who ever followed him.

V09.text: Walter left one more thing on the grave. A chocolate bar. The biggest one they sold.

F084.text: Halloween, 1995. Walter put on his scarecrow costume and handed out candy to every child in Maple Falls. Then he sat by the door, and waited.

F085.text: Eleven forty-five. Eleven forty-six. Eleven forty-seven. The field was quiet. Nobody knocked. Walter sat there until one in the morning.

F086.text: He should have felt relieved. And he was. But he also felt something he didn't expect. He missed him. He missed his little visitor.

F087.text: Walter handed out candy for three more Halloweens. Every year, at eleven forty-seven, he looked at the door. And every year, nobody knocked.

F088.text: In the spring of 1998, Walter Greene passed away peacefully in his armchair, with the window open to the field. He was seventy-eight.

F089.text: Half the town came to say goodbye. Grown men and women who had once gotten caramel apples from the scarecrow on Orchard Lane.

F090.text: Somebody left his old straw hat on the steps of the church. Nobody knew who. Nobody remembered bringing it. But nobody moved it, either.

F091.text: That summer, the white farmhouse on Orchard Lane was sold to a young family from Boston. The Morales family. Two parents and an eight-year-old girl named Sofia.

F092.text: They loved the house. The big porch. The swing. The field out back, where Sofia played all summer long.

F093.text: The neighbors told them about Walter. The scarecrow. The caramel apples. They said Orchard Lane had always been the best street for Halloween.

F094.text: So on Halloween, 1998, the Morales family carved twelve pumpkins, and turned on every light on the porch. Sofia dressed up as a witch.

F095.text: The kids came from all over town. It was a wonderful night. By eleven, Sofia had fallen asleep on the couch in her witch hat.

F096.text: Her mother, Elena, was cleaning up the kitchen when she heard it. Three soft knocks at the front door. She looked at the clock. It was eleven forty-seven.

V10.text: On the porch stood two trick-or-treaters. A small one in a pumpkin mask. And a tall scarecrow.

F097.text: The tall one wore a battered straw hat and a patched denim jacket, with straw sticking out of the sleeves. Its face was hidden under the brim.

F098.text: The small one held out an old white pillowcase. The tall one held out its hand. It was an old man's hand, wrinkled and gentle.

F099.text: Elena didn't scream. She said later she couldn't explain it, but she wasn't afraid. She put a chocolate bar in each of their hands.

F100.text: The scarecrow tipped its straw hat to her. Then the two of them turned and walked down the porch steps, side by side, toward the field.

V11.text: They walked into the field together, the old man and the boy. And halfway across, they were gone.

F101.text: In the morning, Elena went out to the field. The frost was untouched. No footprints. Just two chocolate wrappers, folded neatly on the fence post.

F102.text: She told the neighbors. The old woman next door started to cry, then laughed. Walter always said he'd go trick-or-treating someday, she said.

F103.text: The Morales family still lives in the white house on Orchard Lane. And every Halloween, they keep the porch light on until midnight.

F104.text: Sofia is grown now. But she still comes home every October thirty-first, and sits on the porch swing with a bowl of the biggest chocolate bars in town.

F105.text: At eleven forty-seven, there are always three soft knocks. Two trick-or-treaters. A small one in a pumpkin mask. A tall one in a straw hat.

F106.text: They never say trick or treat. They never say thank you. But the scarecrow always tips his hat. And the boy always waves goodbye.

F107.text: People in Maple Falls don't talk about it much. But on Halloween, nobody on Orchard Lane turns their porch light off before midnight.

F108.text: Because they know that somewhere out there, two old friends are still walking from house to house. Just like they always wanted to.

F109.text: So this Halloween, if you're handing out candy late, and you hear three soft knocks close to midnight, don't be afraid.

V12.text: Just leave the porch light on a little longer. Somebody's still out there, trick-or-treating.

F110.text: And if the smaller one holds out an old white pillowcase, give it something sweet. He waited a very long time for that one last house.

F111.text: Happy Halloween. Leave your porch light on until midnight. And if you hear three soft knocks at eleven forty-seven, you'll know who it is.
